narrationScript: Now, if we break our data into multiple tables to achieve all this wonderful normalization, how do we get a complete picture of information that spans across these tables? This is where SQL JOINs come in. A JOIN clause is used to combine rows from two or more tables based on a related column between them. It's how you reconstruct the full view of your data after you've normalized it. Let's look at the two most common types: INNER JOIN and LEFT JOIN. An INNER JOIN returns only the rows where there is a match in *both* tables based on the specified join condition. Think of it like the intersection of two sets. If a student has no enrollments, or an enrollment has no matching student, those records will simply not appear in the result. In contrast, a LEFT JOIN, sometimes called a LEFT OUTER JOIN, returns *all* rows from the 'left' table – that's the first table listed in your FROM clause – and only the matching rows from the 'right' table. If there's no match in the right table for a record from the left table, the columns from the right table will simply have NULL values. This is incredibly useful when you want to see everything from one table, even if it doesn't have a corresponding record in the other.
